title: The Golden Rule in many faiths
keywords: treat others as you want to be treated
examples: Which religions have the Golden Rule?
What did Hillel say about the Torah on one foot?

explain.say: The Golden Rule says: treat others the way you would like to be treated. It is sometimes called the ethic of reciprocity, and some form of it is found in almost every religion and culture.

draw.text: Treat others as you would like to be treated
Reciprocity: what goes out to others, you would wish for yourself

explain.say: Here it is in different traditions, in words like these. Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism and Confucianism each put the same idea in their own way.

items: Judaism | What is hateful to you, do not do to others
Christianity | Do to others as you would have them do to you
Islam | Wish for your brother what you wish for yourself
Hinduism | Do not do to others what would hurt you
Buddhism | Hurt not others in ways you would find hurtful
Confucianism | Do not impose on others what you do not want

draw.text: Each tradition explains it in its own words and stories

explain.say: A famous Jewish story tells of a man who asked the teacher Hillel to explain the whole Torah while standing on one foot. Hillel said: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour; that is the whole Torah, the rest is commentary, now go and learn.

draw.value: What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Go and learn.
draw.label: Hillel, in the Talmud, Shabbat 31a

draw.text: Jesus, in the Sermon on the Mount: do to others what you would have them do to you

explain.say: Some versions say what to do: treat others well. Others say what not to do: do not harm others in ways you would not want. Both point to the same habit of putting yourself in someone else's place.

a: Do to others as you would have them do to you
Found in the Gospels and the hadith
b: Do not do what you would hate
Found in Hillel, Confucius, the Mahabharata

draw.text: The negative form is sometimes called the silver rule

explain.say: These traditions began far apart, in Jerusalem, Mecca, India and China, often with no contact with one another. Yet they reached a remarkably similar idea about how to treat people.

draw.label: The Golden Rule appears in faiths born far apart

explain.say: Using the rule takes imagination: notice how someone feels, picture yourself in their place, and ask how you would want to be treated. Some people add that we should also ask others what they themselves would like.

items: Ask how you would want to be treated

draw.text: Ask others too: people do not all want the same things

faq.a: The Golden Rule is the idea that you should treat other people the way you would like to be treated yourself. It is found, in some form, in almost every major religion and in many philosophies.
asks: What does treat others as you want to be treated mean?
Explain the Golden Rule
What is the ethic of reciprocity?

faq.q: Which religions have the Golden Rule?
faq.a: Versions of it appear in Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism, Jainism, Confucianism and Taoism, as well as in ancient Greek thought. Each expresses it in its own words.
asks: Is the Golden Rule in every religion?
Which faiths teach treat others as you want to be treated?
Do all religions agree on the Golden Rule?

faq.q: What does Christianity say about the Golden Rule?
faq.a: In the Sermon on the Mount, in Matthew's Gospel, Jesus teaches: do to others what you would have them do to you, for this sums up the Law and the Prophets. Luke's Gospel has a similar saying.
asks: What did Jesus say about treating others?
Where is the Golden Rule in the Bible?
Do unto others as you would have them do unto you

faq.q: What does Judaism say about the Golden Rule?
faq.a: The Torah commands, love your neighbour as yourself, in Leviticus chapter 19. The teacher Hillel later summed up the Torah as: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour; the rest is commentary.
asks: Where does love your neighbour as yourself come from?
What did Hillel say?
Is the Golden Rule in the Torah?

faq.q: What did Hillel say about the Torah on one foot?
faq.a: The Talmud tells that a man asked Hillel to teach him the whole Torah while he stood on one foot. Hillel answered: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour; that is the whole Torah, the rest is commentary; go and learn.
asks: What is the story of Hillel and the man on one foot?
Who was Hillel?
How did Hillel summarise the Torah?

faq.q: What does Islam say about the Golden Rule?
faq.a: A well known hadith, a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, teaches that none of you truly believes until he wishes for his brother what he wishes for himself. Many Muslims read brother here as including all people.
asks: Is the Golden Rule in Islam?
What hadith is like the Golden Rule?
What did the Prophet Muhammad say about treating others?

faq.q: What does Hinduism say about the Golden Rule?
faq.a: The Mahabharata teaches that one should never do to another what one would find hurtful to oneself, and calls this, in brief, the essence of dharma.
asks: Is the Golden Rule in the Mahabharata?
What do Hindu scriptures say about treating others?
Is there a Golden Rule in Hinduism?

faq.q: What does Buddhism say about the Golden Rule?
faq.a: Buddhist texts teach: hurt not others in ways that you yourself would find hurtful. The Dhammapada adds that all beings fear pain and love life, so, comparing others with yourself, you should not harm them.
asks: Is the Golden Rule in Buddhism?
What did the Buddha say about harming others?
What does the Dhammapada say about treating others?

faq.q: What does Confucius say about the Golden Rule?
faq.a: When a student asked for one word to guide a whole life, Confucius chose reciprocity, and explained: do not impose on others what you do not want for yourself. This is in the Analects.
asks: What is shu in Confucianism?
Did Confucius teach the Golden Rule?
What is the Confucian Golden Rule?

faq.q: What does Sikhism say about the Golden Rule?
faq.a: The Guru Granth Sahib teaches seeing the one Creator in everyone, so no one is a stranger. One hymn says: I am a stranger to no one, and no one is a stranger to me.
asks: Is the Golden Rule in Sikhism?
What does the Guru Granth Sahib say about others?
How do Sikhs treat others?

faq.a: The Golden Rule is often stated positively: do to others what you want for yourself. The Silver Rule is the negative form: do not do to others what you would not want, as Hillel and Confucius put it.
asks: How is the Silver Rule different from the Golden Rule?
Positive and negative forms of the Golden Rule
Is do not do to others the same as the Golden Rule?

faq.q: Why is it called the Golden Rule?
faq.a: The name became common in English in the 1600s, calling it golden because it was seen as the most precious rule for living. The idea itself is thousands of years older than the name.
asks: Where does the name Golden Rule come from?
Who named the Golden Rule?
Why golden?

faq.q: Does the Golden Rule always work?
faq.a: Thinkers point out that people do not all want the same things, so treating others exactly as you would like may not suit them. Many add that the heart of the rule is empathy: imagining their place and caring about what they need.
asks: What are problems with the Golden Rule?
What is the platinum rule?
Should I treat others how they want to be treated?

faq.q: Why do so many religions have the Golden Rule?
faq.a: People everywhere live together and need trust, fairness and kindness, so many traditions reached the same insight. In 1993 the Parliament of the World's Religions placed it at the heart of its Declaration Toward a Global Ethic.
asks: Why do religions agree on the Golden Rule?
Is the Golden Rule universal?
What is the Global Ethic?

facts: Leviticus chapter 19 contains the command: love your neighbour as yourself.
In the Talmud, Hillel summarises the Torah as: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour.
In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus teaches: do to others what you would have them do to you.
In the Analects 15.24, Confucius says: do not impose on others what you do not want for yourself.
The 1993 Declaration Toward a Global Ethic of the Parliament of the World's Religions placed the Golden Rule at its heart.

options.say: Whoever has the gold makes the rules

quiz.why: The Golden Rule asks us to treat others the way we would want to be treated ourselves.

wrong.1: That is a joke about power, not the Golden Rule taught by the world's faiths.
wrong.2: The Golden Rule asks you to think of others as you think of yourself.

quiz.say: A new student sits alone at lunch. You remember how lonely you felt on your first day. What would the Golden Rule suggest?
quiz.show: A new student sits alone. What does the Golden Rule suggest?

options.show: Invite them to sit with you
options.say: Invite them to sit with you

options.show: Ignore them, it is not your problem
options.say: Ignore them, it is not your problem

options.show: Wait for a teacher to help
options.say: Wait for a teacher to help

quiz.why: You would have wanted someone to include you, so the Golden Rule suggests including them.

wrong.1: Ignoring them is not how you would want to be treated in their place.
wrong.2: A teacher may help, but the Golden Rule asks what you yourself can do.

quiz.say: Faiths that began in Jerusalem, Arabia, India and China, often with no contact, all teach a form of the Golden Rule. What might this suggest?
quiz.show: Why might faiths far apart share the Golden Rule?

options.show: It reflects a shared human need for fairness
options.say: It reflects a shared human need for fairness and kindness

options.show: One book was copied by all the others
options.say: One book was copied by all the others

options.show: It is only a modern idea
options.say: It is only a modern idea

quiz.why: People everywhere live in communities and need trust and kindness, so many traditions reached a similar insight independently.

wrong.1: Many of these traditions developed separately; the idea appears in texts with no shared source.
wrong.2: It is ancient, found in texts more than two thousand years old.
